claim: Bacillus alcalophilus AV was initially isolated from human feces.
source: Among the first alkaliphilic extremophiles described in the literature, the gram-positive, rod-shaped Bacillus alcalophilus AV was initially isolated from human feces (Vedder, 1934).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vedder, 1934

claim: NsvBa currents from transfected HEK293T cells were robust at approximately 119 pA/pF in 150 mM extracellular Na+.
source: Currents from NsvBa-transfected HEK293T cells were robust (≈119 pA/pF in 150 mM extracellular [Na+]) with voltage-dependent activation and inactivation similar to NaChBac (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements from patch clamp recordings

claim: The time constant of NsvBa Na+ current inactivation measured at 0 mV was 42 ms.
source: The time constant of NsvBa Na+ current inactivation (τinact) measured at 0 mV was 42 ms, ∼2 times faster than NaChBac (78 ms) but ∼6 times slower than NavMs (7 ms, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: NsvBa Na+ current inactivation is approximately 2 times faster than NaChBac.
source: The time constant of NsvBa Na+ current inactivation (τinact) measured at 0 mV was 42 ms, ∼2 times faster than NaChBac (78 ms) but ∼6 times slower than NavMs (7 ms, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental measurements (42 ms vs 78 ms)

claim: NsvBa Na+ current inactivation is approximately 6 times slower than NavMs.
source: The time constant of NsvBa Na+ current inactivation (τinact) measured at 0 mV was 42 ms, ∼2 times faster than NaChBac (78 ms) but ∼6 times slower than NavMs (7 ms, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental measurements (42 ms vs 7 ms)

claim: The sequence TLESWxxG is conserved in the selectivity filters of prokaryotic Na+ channels.
source: The sequence TLESWxxG is conserved in the selectivity filters of prokaryotic Na+ channels (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1C

claim: The selectivity filter sequence of NsvBa is TLDSWGSG.
source: Although the sequence of NsvBa is homologous to other prokaryotic Nav channels, the selectivity filter sequence (TLDSWGSG) deviates at the high field-strength site (SiteHFS most extracellular site; see Discussion) with an aspartate residue replacing glutamate (D186) and a flexible glycine at an extracellular position (G189).
evidence: Directly stated in the text

claim: NsvBa selectivity filter deviates at the high field-strength site with an aspartate residue replacing glutamate at position D186.
source: Although the sequence of NsvBa is homologous to other prokaryotic Nav channels, the selectivity filter sequence (TLDSWGSG) deviates at the high field-strength site (SiteHFS most extracellular site; see Discussion) with an aspartate residue replacing glutamate (D186) and a flexible glycine at an extracellular position (G189).
evidence: Directly stated in the text based on sequence analysis

claim: NsvBa has a flexible glycine at an extracellular position (G189).
source: Although the sequence of NsvBa is homologous to other prokaryotic Nav channels, the selectivity filter sequence (TLDSWGSG) deviates at the high field-strength site (SiteHFS most extracellular site; see Discussion) with an aspartate residue replacing glutamate (D186) and a flexible glycine at an extracellular position (G189).
evidence: Directly stated in the text based on sequence analysis

claim: G189 and G191 form a 'GxG motif' commonly found in K+-selective and nonselective ion channels.
source: When aligned, G189 and G191 form a 'GxG motif' commonly found in K+-selective (Kv) and nonselective ion channels (e.g., TRP and CNG channels, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment and comparison to known channel families

claim: NsvBa was nonselective and all cations but Cs+ and Mg2+ permeated the pore.
source: Compared to the relatively Na+-selective NaChBac channel, NsvBa was nonselective and all cations but Cs+ and Mg2+ permeated the pore (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: NsvBa Na+ single channel conductance was 30 ± 3 pS.
source: NsvBa Na+ and K+ single channel conductances were equivalent (30 ± 3 pS and 36 ± 3 pS, respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the channel does not distinguish between these ions.
evidence: Supported by single channel recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: NsvBa K+ single channel conductance was 36 ± 3 pS.
source: NsvBa Na+ and K+ single channel conductances were equivalent (30 ± 3 pS and 36 ± 3 pS, respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the channel does not distinguish between these ions.
evidence: Supported by single channel recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: NsvBa does not distinguish between Na+ and K+ ions.
source: NsvBa Na+ and K+ single channel conductances were equivalent (30 ± 3 pS and 36 ± 3 pS, respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the channel does not distinguish between these ions.
evidence: Inferred from equivalent single channel conductances for Na+ and K+

claim: NaChBac and NsvBa channels share 61% amino acid identity.
source: Given the 61% shared amino acid identity between NaChBac and NsvBa channels, we were able to introduce the NaChBac selectivity filter (TLESWASG) into the NsvBa channel to examine two relevant residues, D186E and G189A.
evidence: Directly stated in the text

claim: Introducing the NaChBac selectivity filter (TLESWASG) into NsvBa conferred Na+-selectivity and abrogated all other monovalent and divalent conductances.
source: These changes conferred Na+-selectivity onto the channel and abrogated all other monovalent and divalent conductances (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: The single mutation D186E was sufficient for Na+-selectivity in NsvBa.
source: When tested separately, the single mutation D186E was sufficient for Na+-selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas the single mutation of G189A substantially reduced, but did not entirely abolish, the permeability of K+ and Rb+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The single mutation G189A substantially reduced, but did not entirely abolish, the permeability of K+ and Rb+ in NsvBa.
source: When tested separately, the single mutation D186E was sufficient for Na+-selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), whereas the single mutation of G189A substantially reduced, but did not entirely abolish, the permeability of K+ and Rb+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: The G189A mutant channel still conducted Ca2+ and Ba2+ divalent ions, whereas the D186E mutation did not.
source: Furthermore, the G189A mutant channel still conducted Ca2+ and Ba2+ divalent ions, whereas the D186E mutation did not.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: A glutamate at SiteHFS selects Na+ among other cations.
source: These data suggest that a glutamate at SiteHFS selects Na+ among other cations while the 'GxG motif' likely provides an extracellular K+ or Rb+ ion coordination site, possibly involving the glycine backbone carbonyls as found in the selectivity filter of the potassium and NaK channels (Doyle et al., 1998; Jiang et al., 2002; Alam and Jiang, 2009a; Alam and Jiang 2009b).
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data and supported by citations to structural studies

claim: The 'GxG motif' likely provides an extracellular K+ or Rb+ ion coordination site.
source: These data suggest that a glutamate at SiteHFS selects Na+ among other cations while the 'GxG motif' likely provides an extracellular K+ or Rb+ ion coordination site, possibly involving the glycine backbone carbonyls as found in the selectivity filter of the potassium and NaK channels (Doyle et al., 1998; Jiang et al., 2002; Alam and Jiang, 2009a; Alam and Jiang 2009b).
evidence: Inferred from mutagenesis data and supported by citations to structural studies

claim: When the Na+-selectivity filter of NaChBac (TLESWASG) was mutated at two positions (E192D:A195G) to conform to the NsvBa nonselective filter (TLDSWGSG), ion selectivity was identical to that of NsvBa.
source: When the Na+-selectivity filter of NaChBac (TLESWASG) was mutated at two positions (E192D:A195 G) to conform to the NsvBa nonselective filter (TLDSWGSG), ion selectivity was identical to that of NsvBa (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: The selectivity filter is portable between voltage-gated cation channels in Bacillus species halodurans and alcalophilus AV.
source: This finding illustrates the mutual portability of selectivity between the voltage-gated cation channels in Bacillus species halodurans and alcalophilus AV.
evidence: Inferred from successful transfer of selectivity filter sequences between NaChBac and NsvBa

claim: The selectivity for Na+ ions in vertebrate Nav channels is attributed to an asymmetric ring of 4 amino acids (Asp, Glu, Lys, and Ala: DEKA).
source: The selectivity for Na+ ions in vertebrate Nav channels is attributed to an asymmetric ring of 4 amino acids (Asp, Glu, Lys, and Ala: DEKA) contributed by each of the pore-lining loops of the 4 domains (Catterall, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Catterall, 2012

claim: Voltage gated calcium channels (CaVs) are thought to achieve Ca2+-selectivity by a symmetric ring of 4 glutamate residues (EEEE).
source: Voltage gated calcium channels (CaVs) are thought to achieve Ca2+-selectivity by a symmetric ring of 4 glutamate residues (EEEE), each contributed by one domain of the polypeptide (Hess et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hess et al., 1986

claim: Prokaryotes achieve Na+-selectivity from an apparent 4-fold symmetry of acidic residues, each from a subunit in the homomer.
source: In contrast, prokaryotes achieve Na+-selectivity from an apparent 4-fold symmetry of acidic residues, each from a subunit in the homomer.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of prokaryotic Nav channels

claim: The Na+-selective NaChBac (TLESWASG) filter can be converted into one that prefers the divalents Ba2+ and Ca2+ by introducing acidic residues into three positions in the filter sequence (TLDDWADG).
source: In previous studies, we demonstrated that the Na+-selective NaChBac (TLESWASG) filter could be converted into one that prefers the divalents Ba2+ and Ca2+ by introducing acidic residues into three positions in the filter sequence (TLDDWADG) (Yue et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Yue et al., 2002)

claim: The LDDWADG mutated filter in NsvBa was divalent permeant (Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+) but also had measurable permeability to monovalent cations (including K+ and Rb+).
source: We tested the LDDWADG mutated filter (S187D:G189A:S190D) in the NsvBa channel and confirmed that it was divalent permeant (Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+) but it also had measurable permeability to monovalent cations (including K+ and Rb+), demonstrating that Ca2+-preference achieved by this filter (PCa/PNa∼30, Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) is much lower than mammalian CaV channels (PCa/PNa ≳ 1000) (Tsien et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Ca2+-preference achieved by the LDDWADG filter in NsvBa (PCa/PNa∼30) is much lower than mammalian CaV channels (PCa/PNa ≳ 1000).
source: We tested the LDDWADG mutated filter (S187D:G189A:S190D) in the NsvBa channel and confirmed that it was divalent permeant (Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+) but it also had measurable permeability to monovalent cations (including K+ and Rb+), demonstrating that Ca2+-preference achieved by this filter (PCa/PNa∼30, Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) is much lower than mammalian CaV channels (PCa/PNa ≳ 1000) (Tsien et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Tsien et al., 1987

claim: The selectivity of the LDDWADG filter is more analogous to some members of the TRP channel family, such as TRPV5, TRPV6.
source: Rather, this selectivity is more analogous to some members of the TRP channel family, such as TRPV5, TRPV6 (Owsianik et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Owsianik et al., 2006 and Wu et al., 2010

claim: Alkaliphilic Bacillus are estimated to have very negative resting membrane potentials (Ψrest ≈ −180 mV).
source: Alkaliphilic Bacillus are estimated to have very negative resting membrane potentials (Ψrest ≈ −180 mV), although membrane potentials in bacteria are measured from voltage- sensitive dye studies and variability within populations can be large.
evidence: Based on voltage-sensitive dye studies

claim: The activation threshold for Bacillus sodium channels is approximately −40 mV.
source: Nevertheless, the activation threshold for Bacillus sodium channels is ≈ −40 mV, which is extremely depolarized relative to estimates of Ψrest.
evidence: Based on experimental measurements

claim: Na+ currents from NaChBac and NsvBa are modulated by high extracellular pH.
source: As shown for the Na+-selective channel from Bacillus pseudofirmus OF4 (NavBp) (Ito et al., 2004), Na+ currents from NaChBac and NsvBa are also modulated by high extracellular pH (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Ito et al., 2004

claim: When extracellular pH was increased from 7.4 to 9.4, the peak current increased twofold to fourfold.
source: When extracellular pH was increased from 7.4 to 9.4, the peak current increased twofold to fourfold and the steady state voltage-dependence was negatively shifted by 28–34 mV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: When extracellular pH was increased from 7.4 to 9.4, the steady state voltage-dependence was negatively shifted by 28–34 mV.
source: When extracellular pH was increased from 7.4 to 9.4, the peak current increased twofold to fourfold and the steady state voltage-dependence was negatively shifted by 28–34 mV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: At neutral pH, increasing the temperature shifted the voltage dependence of activation for NsvBa, NaChBac and NavBp channels by −19 to −24 mV.
source: At neutral pH, we observed that increasing the temperature shifted the voltage dependence of activation for these channels by −19 to −24 mV (−62, −55, −51 mV respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: When tested together, temperature and basic pH effects on V1/2 for NsvBa, NaChBac and NavBp were additive, converging on approximately −100 mV.
source: When tested together, temperature and basic pH effects on V1/2 for NsvBa, NaChBac and NavBp were additive, converging on ≈−100 mV (−95, −102, −100 mV respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: NsvBa remains a non-selective channel at higher pH and temperature.
source: Importantly, we determined that the NsvBa remains a non-selective channel at higher pH and temperature, although the Px/PNa for K+ and Ca2+ did increase slightly 2–3 times (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The Q10 for NaChBac and NavBp peak currents was 3.5–4.4 at neutral pH and 3.5–4.1 at basic pH.
source: The Q10 for NaChBac and NavBp peak currents was 3.5–4.4 at neutral pH and 3.5–4.1 at basic pH.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: The voltage-dependence of activation of the hNav1.1 channel was less temperature-sensitive (Q10 = 1.2 and 1.4) than Bacillus Nav channels.
source: In contrast, the voltage-dependence of activation of the hNav1.1 channel was less temperature- (Q10 = 1.2 and 1.4, Figure 6D) and pH- (Δ V1/2 < 8 mV, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) sensitive.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The voltage-dependence of activation of the hNav1.1 channel was less pH-sensitive (Δ V1/2 < 8 mV) than Bacillus Nav channels.
source: In contrast, the voltage-dependence of activation of the hNav1.1 channel was less temperature- (Q10 = 1.2 and 1.4, Figure 6D) and pH- (Δ V1/2 < 8 mV, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) sensitive.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: pH and temperature-induced increases of the peak current and reduction of the voltage-dependence of activation are distinct from eukaryotic Nav channels.
source: Thus, pH and temperature-induced increases of the peak current and reduction of the voltage-dependence of activation are distinct from eukaryotic Nav channels.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Bacillus Nav channels with hNav1.1

claim: Concentrations of lidocaine, nifedipine, and tamoxifen that inhibit heterologously-expressed bacterial Nav channels (NavBp and NsvBa) also block the growth of native Bacillus species (B. pseudofirmus and B. alcalophilus).
source: Concentrations of lidocaine, nifedipine, and tamoxifen that inhibit heterologously-expressed bacterial Nav channels (NavBp and NsvBa) also block the growth of native Bacillus species (B. pseudofirmus and B. alcalophilus).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing drug effects on channels and bacterial growth

claim: All three drugs (lidocaine, nifedipine, and tamoxifen) affected motility for B. pseudofirmus.
source: Although all three drugs affected motility for B. pseudofirmus, only tamoxifen and nifedipine increased tumbling frequency of B. alcalophilus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on bacterial motility

claim: Only tamoxifen and nifedipine increased tumbling frequency of B. alcalophilus.
source: Although all three drugs affected motility for B. pseudofirmus, only tamoxifen and nifedipine increased tumbling frequency of B. alcalophilus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on bacterial motility

claim: B. alcalophilus swim speed was not delayed by the three drugs.
source: However, B. alcalophilus swim speed was not delayed by the three drugs and only tamoxifen and nifedipine increased tumbling frequency (EC50 = 70 μM and 375 μM, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on bacterial motility

claim: The measured half-inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of sodium current and bacterial growth were within a half-log unit.
source: The measured half-inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of sodium current and bacterial growth were within a half-log unit (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that growth inhibition was not an off-target effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Growth inhibition by Nav channel antagonists was not an off-target effect.
source: The measured half-inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of sodium current and bacterial growth were within a half-log unit (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that growth inhibition was not an off-target effect.
evidence: Inferred from the close correspondence between IC50 values for channel block and growth inhibition

claim: Four identical subunits, each containing 6-transmembrane segments, assemble together to form a functional bacterial Nav channel.
source: The full-length structures demonstrate that four identical subunits, each containing 6-transmembrane segments, assemble together to form a functional channel.
evidence: Based on structural studies of prokaryotic Nav channels

claim: The first four transmembrane segments form the voltage sensor (S1–S4) in bacterial Nav channels.
source: The first four transmembrane segments form the voltage sensor (S1–S4) while the fifth and sixth transmembrane segments (S5, S6) form the pore domain.
evidence: Based on structural studies of prokaryotic Nav channels

claim: The fifth and sixth transmembrane segments (S5, S6) form the pore domain in bacterial Nav channels.
source: The first four transmembrane segments form the voltage sensor (S1–S4) while the fifth and sixth transmembrane segments (S5, S6) form the pore domain.
evidence: Based on structural studies of prokaryotic Nav channels

claim: The selectivity filter is scaffolded by two pore helices (P1 and P2) from each subunit.
source: The selectivity filter, which forms critical interactions with the permeating hydrated ions, defines the pore and is scaffolded by two pore helices (P1 and P2) from each subunit.
evidence: Based on structural studies of prokaryotic Nav channels

claim: The first prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channel was cloned from Bacillus halodurans C-125 and was called NaChBac.
source: The first prokaryotic voltage-gated sodium channel, cloned from Bacillus halodurans C-125, was called NaChBac (Na+ Channel of Bacteria) (Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ren et al., 2001

claim: NaV channels from at least 9 bacterial species have been functionally characterized.
source: Since then, NaV channels from at least 9 bacterial species have been functionally characterized.
evidence: Based on review of the literature

claim: All full-length bacterial Nav channels exhibit Na+-selectivity.
source: All full-length channels exhibit Na+-selectivity (Ren et al., 2001; Ito et al., 2004; Koishi et al., 2004; Irie et al., 2010; Ulmschneider et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Growth and motility of the alkaliphilic bacterium Bacillus alcalophilus AV are better supported in K+ rather than Na+ conditions.
source: Growth and motility of the alkaliphilic bacterium Bacillus alcalophilus AV (Vedder, 1934) are better supported in K+ rather than Na+ conditions (Terahara et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Terahara et al., 2012

claim: In alkaliphilic Bacillus, either Na+ or K+ ion can drive the flagellar motor.
source: In alkaliphilic Bacillus, either ion can drive the flagellar motor, and a single mutation in the MotS protein was identified that converted the naturally nonselective MotPS (Na+ or K+) stator into a Na+-selective stator.
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: A single mutation in the MotS protein converted the naturally nonselective MotPS (Na+ or K+) stator into a Na+-selective stator.
source: In alkaliphilic Bacillus, either ion can drive the flagellar motor, and a single mutation in the MotS protein was identified that converted the naturally nonselective MotPS (Na+ or K+) stator into a Na+-selective stator.
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: Bacterial Nav channels provide a source of Na+ ions that drives the stators and maintains ion homeostasis.
source: Presumably, bacterial Nav channels provide a source of Na+ ions that drives the stators and maintains ion homeostasis.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the role of Nav channels

claim: Two full-length prokaryotic Na+ channel crystal structures (NavAb and NavRh) have been solved.
source: To date, two full-length (NavAb and NavRh) (Payandeh et al., 2011, 2012; Zhang et al., 2012) and three pore-only (NavMs, NavAe and NavCt) (McCusker et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2013; Shaya et al., 2014) prokaryotic Na+ channel crystal structures have been solved.
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies

claim: Three pore-only prokaryotic Na+ channel crystal structures (NavMs, NavAe and NavCt) have been solved.
source: To date, two full-length (NavAb and NavRh) (Payandeh et al., 2011, 2012; Zhang et al., 2012) and three pore-only (NavMs, NavAe and NavCt) (McCusker et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2013; Shaya et al., 2014) prokaryotic Na+ channel crystal structures have been solved.
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies

claim: The molecular arrangement that enables Na+-selectivity in prokaryotes might differ from mammalian voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: However, the molecular arrangement that enables Na+-selectivity in prokaryotes might differ from mammalian voltage-gated Na+ channels.
evidence: Speculative statement based on structural differences

claim: It is not clear if structural features that determine ion selectivity in homotetrameric prokaryotic NaV reflect the functionally heterotetrameric eukaryotic sodium channels.
source: Thus, it is not clear if structural features that determine ion selectivity in homotetrameric prokaryotic NaV reflect the functionally heterotetrameric eukaryotic sodium channels.

claim: In soda lakes and other extremely H+-poor (pH 9–12; 1 nM—1 pM [H+]) and Na+-rich environments (up to 500 mM), alkaliphilic prokaryotes couple motility and ion transporters to Na+ rather than H+.
source: In soda lakes and other extremely H+-poor (pH 9–12; 1 nM—1 pM [H+]) and Na+-rich environments (up to 500 mM), alkaliphilic prokaryotes couple motility and ion transporters to Na+ rather than H+.

claim: Most bacteria require the ion-motive forces provided by H+ or Na+ ions that move through the MotAB or MotPS stator to power the rotary motor proteins to drive the motion of the flagella.
source: Most bacteria require the ion-motive forces provided by H+ or Na+ ions that move through the MotAB or MotPS stator to power the rotary motor proteins to drive the motion of the flagella, (Figure 1A) (Ito et al., 2004; Fujinami et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ito et al., 2004 and Fujinami et al., 2009

claim: In alkaliphilic Bacillus, high external pH activates voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav), which allows Na+ to enter and be used as substrate for cation/proton antiporters responsible for cytoplasmic pH homeostasis.
source: In alkaliphilic prokaryotes, high external pH activates voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav), which allows Na+ to enter and be used as substrate for cation/proton antiporters responsible for cytoplasmic pH homeostasis.
evidence: Based on the proposed role of Nav channels in alkaliphilic bacteria

claim: NsvBa is a new member of the prokaryotic voltage-gated Na+ channel family from Bacillus alcalophilus.
source: Here, we describe a new member of the prokaryotic voltage-gated Na+ channel family (NsvBa; Non-selective voltage-gated, Bacillus alcalophilus) that is nonselective among Na+, Ca2+ and K+ ions.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract

claim: NsvBa is nonselective among Na+, Ca2+ and K+ ions.
source: Here, we describe a new member of the prokaryotic voltage-gated Na+ channel family (NsvBa; Non-selective voltage-gated, Bacillus alcalophilus) that is nonselective among Na+, Ca2+ and K+ ions.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data

claim: Mutations in NsvBa can convert the nonselective filter into one that discriminates for Na+ or divalent cations.
source: Mutations in NsvBa can convert the nonselective filter into one that discriminates for Na+ or divalent cations.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data

claim: Filter mutations can confer ion selectivity to other Bacillus Nav channels.

evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data

claim: Increasing pH and temperature shifts the activation threshold of Bacillus Nav channels towards their native resting membrane potential.
source: Increasing pH and temperature shifts their activation threshold towards their native resting membrane potential.

claim: Drugs that target Bacillus Nav channels also block the growth of the bacteria.
source: Furthermore, we find drugs that target Bacillus Nav channels also block the growth of the bacteria.

claim: The selectivity of Bacillus Nav channels can be converted from nonselective, to relatively higher Na+ or Ca2+ selectivity.
source: Through a series of mutations, we showed that the selectivity of Bacillus Nav channels can be converted from nonselective, to relatively higher Na+ or Ca2+ selectivity, suggesting that the filter is readily mutable in evolution to adapt to ionic conditions.

claim: The filter of Bacillus Nav channels is readily mutable in evolution to adapt to ionic conditions.
source: Through a series of mutations, we showed that the selectivity of Bacillus Nav channels can be converted from nonselective, to relatively higher Na+ or Ca2+ selectivity, suggesting that the filter is readily mutable in evolution to adapt to ionic conditions.

claim: These highly adaptable selectivity filters are critical for the Bacillus alkaliphiles, allowing for the habitation of various cation-rich environments in which they presumably evolved.
source: These highly adaptable selectivity filters are critical for the Bacillus alkaliphiles, allowing for the habitation of various cation-rich environments in which they presumably evolved.

claim: It is anticipated that the ion-specificity of at least some antiporters will parallel that of the major coupling ions for the voltage-gated channels that provide a significant amount of their cytoplasmic substrate.
source: It is anticipated that the ion-specificity of at least some antiporters will parallel that of the major coupling ions for the voltage-gated channels that provide a significant amount of their cytoplasmic substrate.

claim: No Na+ ions reside within the filter of the wild type NavAb crystal structures.
source: Although no Na+ ions reside within the filter of the wild type NavAb crystal structures, 3 Na+ coordinating sites were proposed: glutamate side chains form a high-field-strength site (SiteHFS) near the extracellular end of the filter, while backbone carbonyls of Leu and Thr comprise central (SiteCEN) and inner sites (SiteIN) (Payandeh et al., 2011).

claim: 3 Na+ coordinating sites were proposed in NavAb: SiteHFS, SiteCEN, and SiteIN.
source: Although no Na+ ions reside within the filter of the wild type NavAb crystal structures, 3 Na+ coordinating sites were proposed: glutamate side chains form a high-field-strength site (SiteHFS) near the extracellular end of the filter, while backbone carbonyls of Leu and Thr comprise central (SiteCEN) and inner sites (SiteIN) (Payandeh et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on structural analysis cited from Payandeh et al., 2011

claim: In the CavAb structure, 3 hydrated Ca2+ ions were found coordinated within the filter.
source: In the CavAb structure, 3 hydrated Ca2+ ions were found coordinated within the filter and 3 sites (Sites 1–3) proposed within the filter.
evidence: Based on structural analysis

claim: Site 1 in CavAb is formed by 4 Asp carboxyl side chains, equivalent to positions Ser 196 in NaChBac and Ser 190 in NsvBa.
source: Site 1, the one closest to the extracellular surface, is formed by 4 Asp carboxyl side chains, equivalent to positions Ser 196 in NaChBac and Ser 190 in NsvBa.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and sequence alignment

claim: Site 2 in CavAb (equivalent to SiteHFS in NavAb) is formed by four side chain carboxyls and four backbone carbonyls from equivalent residues of Glu 192 in NaChBac and Asp 186 in NsvBa.
source: Site 2 (equivalent to SiteHFS in the wt NavAb crystal structure) is formed by four side chain carboxyls and four backbone carbonyls from equivalent residues of Glu 192 in NaChBac and Asp 186 in NsvBa.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and sequence alignment

claim: The shorter side chain of the NsvBa Asp acidic residue at site 2 is correlated with decreased Na+-selectivity.
source: Our data suggest that the shorter side chain of the NsvBa Asp acidic residue at site 2 is correlated with decreased Na+-selectivity, but Na+ selectivity can be artificially endowed when replaced by a Glu (D186E) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
